messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 27
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Physical Therapist
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Cologne/Perfume): A specific perfume or cologne, Somatic (Pain): Physical pain in a part of the body, Sexual Situations: Sexual situations or intimacy
  Maladaptive Strategies: Dissociation: I pretend it happened to someone else, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury
  Threat: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Omar, a 27-year-old married physical therapist from a Middle Eastern family, came to understand his difficulties as beginning after a sexual assault that happened when he was leaving a social gathering with people he knew. The event itself was brief but disorganizing: there was sudden unwanted sexual contact, a sense of being overpowered, and a shock that left him unable to make sense of what was happening until it was over. In the days afterward, he found himself replaying the memory only in fragments and then pushing it away as soon as it appeared. He would tell himself that it had happened to someone else, as though distancing the scene could make it less real. At other times he made a deliberate effort not to think about it at all, because once he started, the details felt too immediate and humiliating to tolerate. What lingered most sharply was not only the act itself but how violated his body felt, and he developed a habit of checking his body constantly for signs of danger or injury, almost reflexively scanning himself whenever he was alone.

Over the following weeks, Omar noticed that certain ordinary experiences could bring the memory rushing back without warning. A particular perfume or cologne was especially potent; if someone in a store, elevator, or waiting room wore the same type of scent, he would go rigid and feel instantly back in the atmosphere of the assault. Because he worked as a physical therapist, he could not always control when he encountered bodily pain in others or when he himself felt discomfort. Any pain in a part of the body, even if minor, drew his attention in a way that felt urgent and threatening, as though his body might be signaling that something was wrong again. At work, when a patient unexpectedly flinched, reached, or shifted quickly beside him on the treatment table, he reacted with visible alarm before he could stop himself. He was embarrassed by how jumpy he had become, especially because his job required calm physical contact and confidence. A sudden touch from a colleague on the shoulder, even in a harmless context, made him startle sharply and then try to cover it with a forced smile. He became increasingly aware of his own body in the clinic, not only because of the pain he noticed but because he was always checking, as if vigilance might keep him safe from another shock.

The assault also altered how he experienced intimacy with his wife. Before the trauma, he had seen their sexual relationship as private and reassuring; afterward, sexual situations became one of the clearest triggers for him. He would tense as soon as intimacy seemed likely, and even when he wanted closeness, he found himself pulled into alarm by the anticipation of touch and vulnerability. He felt ashamed of what had happened to his body and struggled with the sense that the experience had marked him in a way he could not undo. He had come to believe that he could not rely on himself, not because he lacked willpower, but because his reactions felt unpredictable and outside his control. That belief showed up in small but painful moments: he would withdraw at times he wanted to be present, second-guess his own comfort, or abruptly stop a conversation about intimacy because he feared becoming overwhelmed. At the same time, he told himself that he would never be able to feel normal emotions again. He noticed that even when he was with people he loved, his emotions felt flattened, distant, or not fully his own, and this loss frightened him nearly as much as the memory itself.

As months passed, Omar’s efforts to keep the experience at a distance became part of daily life. He avoided thinking about it as much as possible, but the avoidance had its own cost: the assault remained unfinished in his mind, something he had to circle around rather than name directly. He continued working, but he did so with a constant undercurrent of alertness, especially in situations that involved touch, movement nearby, bodily discomfort, or the scent that reminded him of the attack. Home was not entirely restful either, because intimacy with his wife could suddenly feel like stepping into danger. He had not sought help immediately, in part because he felt ashamed and in part because he feared that speaking about it would make the reality more complete. What finally brought him to treatment was the accumulation of these moments—being startled at work by a hand on his arm, feeling his body tense at the wrong scent, and recognizing that he was increasingly living as though his own reactions could not be trusted. He came hoping to regain some sense of steadiness in his body and mind, and fearing that if nothing changed, he would remain cut off from the emotions and closeness that mattered most to him.
